strategy.summary: Small founder-owned Czech machining shop and our single source for Adapter piece HI. We own the tooling. It is financially sound and only lightly dependent on us. The owner decides personally, values partnership (he cites the 2022 price hold) and costs from a spreadsheet that is two years out of date. The sales director has signalled a review of small accounts. Real cost pressure from cold-drawn bars has built up since the 2026 price was held flat. Quality is weak and not improving, and delivery has improved but is still below the contract target. Our best levers are growing volume, its own history of settling below its ask, quality, and partnership gestures (on-time payment, a longer commitment). Evidence is thin: there is no should-cost, no rival quote and only short notes on the owner.

price_view.reasoning: There is no should-cost. Bar costs rose materially, and the price was held flat for 2026 and is below 2023. Holding the current price or settling a small increase is realistic. A cut has no cost basis apart from quality. Its pattern of settling below its ask suggests that a modest ask can be brought near zero with volume and length.

findings.text: No should-cost exists for part 320050 and there are no competing quotes or RFQs, so we cannot measure how far 15.88 sits above full cost. The economics rest only on index drivers and price history, which is thin evidence.

The weighted index drivers point to cost pressure of roughly +4.6% over 12 months. The main parts are cold-drawn bars (+12.3%, weight 0.31, about +3.8% on price) and labour (+2.7%, weight 0.36, about +0.96%). Power (-3.7%, weight 0.03, about -0.11%) barely offsets them. The weights cover only 70% of cost, and the remaining 30% (overhead and margin) carries no index.

Bar prices have turned. PPI-C2431 is down 2.3% from its 2026-06 peak and still 7.5% below its 2022-06 all-time high. The 12-month jump compares against a 36-month low in 2025-06/08, so the rise is partly a rebound. Labour has been flat since 2026-04.

Price history is 16.35 (2023), 15.46 (2024, -5.4%), 15.88 (2025, +2.7%) and 15.88 (2026, unchanged). The price is 2.9% below 2023, while bar costs are below their 2022 peak and power is down 43.5% from its high. The 2024 cut tracked falling input costs, but 2026 was held flat despite rising bars, so the supplier has a credible claim of absorbing roughly +4% since its last change.

The owner prices from a spreadsheet last updated about two years ago. He may not know the current index levels, and the bar rise he has not yet claimed is the biggest exposure. Our own index figures will show the rise as well as the recent fall, so we should cite only the facts that help us, such as the decline since the June peak and power.

Room on price: holding 15.88 is defensible. The supplier's past pattern is asking +1.5% and settling -0.9%; it last asked +2.8% and settled 0%. If it asks for an increase, a settlement of 0 to +1.5% is plausible to expect. A price cut is hard to justify on cost grounds. Its quality (1531 ppm against a peer median of 457) and the volume rise (5880 to 6650) are better levers than costs. Prices are fixed per calendar year under ctr:4600070270#3.1 with 90 days' notice, so a 2027 change needed notice by about early October 2026.

findings.text: Small founder-owned shop (30 staff, 2-5 M EUR turnover). The owner decides and negotiates in person, so expect personal, relationship-driven reasoning rather than a corporate approval ladder. A sales director exists but plays a secondary role.

The owner invokes past sacrifice: in 2022 he kept supplying at the old price for a quarter, and he expects 'partnership' in return. This is a sensitivity. Acknowledge it explicitly, or he will read hard bargaining as ingratitude.

His costing is stale. He works from his own spreadsheet, last updated about two years ago, and asked where our index figures come from. We can steer the cost discussion with official 12-month index data. He may also be unaware of falls since the peak (cold-drawn bars -7.5% from the 2022 high, power down), but cold-drawn bars are up +12.3% over 12 months, which helps him if he updates.

Risk of deprioritisation. The sales director said they are reviewing small accounts to focus on customers with volume. We are about 2.7% of their turnover (EUR 93k), and the part is single-sourced (though we own the tooling). Rising volume (6650 vs 5880) is our best counter-signal.
Financially sound and stable: equity ratio 44.8%, credit index 245 unchanged. There is no stress to exploit, and they can afford to walk away. Cash is not obviously a pressing need.

We pay late: 85.3% of invoices late, on average 5.8 days after due, maximum 13 days. This is a legitimate grievance he can raise, and paying on time or faster is a cheap concession that would signal partnership.

They show operational initiative, for example switching to returnable boxes. They have a history of settling well below their ask. Performance is weak: quality 1531 ppm vs a peer median of 457, and on-time delivery 84.6%, though improved from 68%.
The evidence is thin: there is no news, and the documents are only four short notes. The owner's priorities are inferred from brief remarks.

findings.text: Framework agreement ctr:4600070270 covers only part:320050, runs 2025-07-01 to 2027-06-30 and auto-extends 12 months unless terminated with 90 days' notice. To stop the extension, notice must be given by 2027-04-01, so a credible exit is still open.

Prices are fixed per calendar year. Any change needs written notice at least 90 days before year end, i.e. by about 2026-10-02 for 2027. If no notice arrives in time, the 2026 price of 15.88 stays for 2027.

Other contract terms: payment 45 days net (shorter than our 60-day standard, already a benefit to them); EXW with 42-day lead time; quality agreement with a 95% on-time target and EUR 150 flat fee per complaint.

History shows it settles well below its ask. Three renewals:
- 2023-11: asked -4.1%, settled -5.4%
- 2024-12: asked +5.8%, settled +2.7%
- 2025-12: asked +2.8%, settled 0%
The average gap is about 2.4 pp, and the price is down 2.9% since 2023 (16.35 to 15.88).

Mutual dependency is modest on both sides:
- It is our single source at 100% quota, approved since 2018.
- We own the tooling, so the part can be moved.
- Our spend (~EUR 93k) is about 2.7% of its turnover.
- It is financially sound and has signalled it is reviewing small accounts.

Performance is below contract:
- On-time delivery 84.6% against the 95% target, though improved from 68%.
- 1531 ppm against a peer median of 457 ppm; complaints were recharged under clause 6.1.
This supports holding the price or adding quality terms.
Evidence is thin on alternative sources: no RFQ history, and no qualified second source is known. Also, we pay 5.8 days late on average, which weakens any request to extend payment terms.

findings.text: Delivery has improved steadily but is still below the 95% target: rolling OTD against the requested date rose from 60.9% (2024Q4) to 84.6% (2026Q3), and against its own confirmed date it is 88.5%. That 84.6% equals the peers' median. When it is late, it is late by a lot: on average 17.8 days in the last 12 months (max 26), against a 42-day lead time. The trend is credit to it; the gap to target is our argument.

Quality is its weak point and is not improving. Rolling ppm is 1531 against a peers' median of 457 (about 3.3x). It has stayed between 880 and 1937 for two years: 1590 a year ago and 1937 at the 2026Q1 peak. Of 21 notifications on part:320050, 20 were supplier-caused. Defects recur: porosity, leakage at test, burrs, missing marking and wrong material certificates come back again and again, so the 8D actions do not seem to stick. 8D closures take 1-3 months, and one 8D was overdue in 2025Q4.

The defect cost recovered is small and incomplete: EUR 2,100 recharged over 20 supplier-caused notifications at EUR 150 flat. Several supplier-caused notifications were not recharged (e.g. qn:20004838, qn:20004969, qn:20004679, qn:20004656). Our real cost of sorting, testing and returns is likely higher. This supports a ppm commitment or a higher chargeback rather than a price argument alone.

Our volume outlook is growing and is shared with the supplier: the 2026-09 forecast is 6650 pcs for the next 12 months against 5880 ordered in the last 12 months (+13%). Forecasts have trended up since 2025-12. Monthly demand is lumpy (240 pcs in 2027-08, 810 pcs in 2027-09). The supplier said it will focus on customers with volume, so this growth is a lever for price and terms.

The price has been flat at 15.88 since 2025 (16.35 in 2023, 15.46 in 2024). Its last renewal ask was +2.8% and settled at 0%. The recent purchase orders are confirmed on the requested date. There were 7 rush lines in the order history, which may support its view that our flexibility demands cost it something.

Our dependency is real: it is the single approved source for part:320050, with a 100% quota. Our spend is only about 2.7% of its turnover, so a lever based on the size of our account is weak. Because we own the tooling, a move to another source is possible, but it would take time.

arguments.text: Cold-drawn bar, our main material (C45), has risen sharply. Cold drawing of bars is +12.3 % year on year and makes up about 31 % of the cost. We held the price flat for 2026, so we have absorbed this rise for a full year.

Today's price of 15.88 is below the 2023 price of 16.35, even after labour and steel rose. The last renewal was settled at 0 % against our 2.8 % ask, and in 2023 we accepted -5.4 %. We have given more than we have taken.
Labour costs are +2.7 % and make up about 36 % of the cost.
Partnership: in 2022 we kept supplying at the old price for a quarter. We expect reciprocity now.
Delivery is clearly improving. On-time delivery against the requested date rose from 60.9 % to 84.6 %, the score rose to 84.7, and we switched to returnable packaging.
Hollerau pays late: 85 % of invoices are paid late, on average 5.8 days after the due date. That is a real cost to a small shop.

weak_points: Quality: about 1,500 ppm, 20 supplier-caused complaints, no improvement, recurring porosity and wrong material certificates, and 8D reports that take long to close.
On-time delivery of 84.6 % is still below the 95 % contract target.
Power prices are down 43 % on 2022 and -3.7 % year on year. Our spreadsheet is two years old, so we cannot fully back our cost figures.
Hollerau owns the tooling and could move the part.
The price is fixed per calendar year and needs 90 days' written notice before year end, so the timing is tight.
Our own remark that we are reviewing small accounts may look like a bluff, since we want this volume.
Copper (+48 %) and electronics (+41 %) do not apply to our part and must not be cited.
wants: A price increase of roughly 3-4 %, with a realistic settlement around 2 %.
A binding annual volume of about 6,600 pcs, matching the forecast.
Extension of the contract to 24 months or more.
On-time payment at 45 days, or 30 days in exchange for a price concession.
An index clause on cold-drawn bar (PPI-C2431) as an alternative to a fixed increase.
Relief from the EUR 150 chargeback per complaint, or a jointly agreed quality plan instead.
red_lines: No price cut: 15.88 is already below 2023 and costs have risen.
No ppm commitment that is unrealistic for our process without support.
No second flat year without at least a volume or length commitment in return.
red_team.opening: Thank Hollerau for the growing volumes and acknowledge the delivery improvements. Point to the cold-drawn bar rise (+12.3 %, ~31 % of cost) and to the 2026 price we held flat, which is below the 2023 price. Ask for +4.5 % effective 2027-01-01, or alternatively +2.5 % with a bar index clause. Signal flexibility if Hollerau commits to a binding 6,600 pcs per year, a 24-month extension and payment on time.

rebuttals.answer: You are right that cold-drawn bar has risen over the year and that you held the price for this year; we recognise that. To keep it in proportion: the bar index has eased again from its recent peak, it is roughly a third of the part's cost, and power, another of your inputs, has fallen over the same period. The bar increase therefore supports a small adjustment at most, not a large one, and we would like to agree on the official index series together rather than work from older internal figures.

We acknowledge the price today sits below its first level and that the last renewal closed flat. Over the same years the volume we order has grown and keeps growing, and our renewals have regularly settled well below the opening ask on both sides, which is how these talks normally conclude. The current price is the fair anchor, and a higher, steadier volume is what we can give in return.

The labour index figure is correct, and labour is a significant share of the cost. Weighted by that share, though, it moves the price by well under one percent, and partly offsetting inputs such as power have fallen. We are glad to take it into account as part of a balanced overall view.

We remember the price hold and value it sincerely; it is one reason we have kept you as our sole source on this part for so many years. We want to reciprocate in ways that help you plan: a longer framework, a binding volume within our growing need, and a firm commitment to paying on time. That is the kind of partnership we would like to build on.

Your delivery improvement is real and we thank your team for it, and the switch to returnable boxes was a welcome initiative. On-time delivery is now around the peer median but still clearly short of the contract target, so we see it as good progress rather than grounds for a higher price. We would like to keep that momentum going together.

That is a fair point and we accept it: our payments have run a few days past due too often. We will commit to paying on the agreed terms going forward, which we see as part of our side of the partnership; your payment terms are already shorter than our usual standard.

press: We would value your view on how the recurring porosity, marking and certificate issues on this part will be resolved, since its defect rate remains well above what we see from comparable suppliers.
Could we agree a ppm target together as part of a longer framework, so that quality and volume move forward hand in hand?
We appreciate the delivery progress and would like to agree how we reach the contract on-time target over the coming year.
Under our framework the price runs per calendar year with written notice before year end, so it would help to understand how you see the timing for any change.
Since power costs have fallen over the year, we suggest we both work from the same official index series when we review cost drivers.
Given our growing forecast volume, we hope our account fits well within the customers you are choosing to focus on.
